title: God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen
about: God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen is one of the oldest English carols still sung today. Its words were sold on cheap printed sheets in London from about 1760. William Sandys printed the tune in his book of Christmas carols in 1833. Its first line once meant: may God grant you peace and happiness.
funFact: In Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol, a boy sings this carol at Scrooge's keyhole. Scrooge chases him away with a ruler.

practice.text: Play the first five bars with the right hand alone, and let the song wait for each note.
Play bars 10 to 14 with the right hand alone, where the tune climbs to the high A.
Now the left hand alone. It holds one low note or an open fifth at a time.
Put both hands together on the whole song, slowly.
Play the whole song with both hands at full speed.

tips.text: Your thumb starts on the A below middle C, and the little finger rests on E.
Lift the hand a moment after the A, and let the thumb drop onto the G below it.
This is the refrain. Let it ring out a little louder than the verse.

tricky.text: Fingers 4 and 5 climb to the high A. Lift the hand, and the little finger lands on E below it.
Fingers 3, 2 and 1 walk down to A. Lift the hand, and the thumb drops onto G.
Fingers 3, 2 and 1 walk down to C. Lift the hand, and finger 2 lands on B.

practice.text: Play the left hand alone: a low note, then the notes above it, twice in each bar.
Play bars 2 to 5 with the right hand alone. The hand moves twice on the way.
Play bars 7 and 8 with the right hand alone, where a repeated note helps the hand move.
Play the whole song with both hands, a little slower than written.
Now play it at full speed.

tips.text: Finger 4 slides down from D to C. In the next bar, the thumb slides up from G to A.
Change finger on the second of the two quick A's and D's. The hand then moves without a jump.
C and B share one beat. Count one-and, and play them as two quick, even steps.

tricky.text: Fingers 4 and 5 climb to the high A. Then the little finger jumps down to E, and finger 4 takes D.
The little finger jumps from the high A down to E. The hand then walks down to B.
Finger 2 slides up from D to E. Then each finger takes the next key, up to the high A.

practice.text: Play the left hand alone until the broken chords roll by themselves: low, high, middle, high.
Play bars 3 and 4 with the right hand alone, where the fingers cross each way.
Join the hands on the first nine bars, slowly.
Play the whole song with both hands at three-quarter speed.
Now play it at full speed.

tips.text: Keep the broken chords soft, so the tune sings above them.
Going down, finger 3 crosses over the thumb onto B. Going up, the thumb tucks under onto C.
The thumb tucks under for E, and the hand climbs to the high A.

tricky.text: The thumb tucks under onto E. Fingers 2 and 3 climb, and the little finger reaches the high A.
Finger 3 drops to E and walks down to C. Then finger 2 crosses over the thumb onto B.
Finger 2 crosses over the thumb onto C. At the end of the bar, the thumb tucks under for C.

practice.text: Play the stride bass alone: jump down for the low octave, then back up for the chord.
Play the right hand alone on bars 4 to 6, and keep the quick turn light.
Join the hands on the first nine bars at half speed.
Play the whole song with both hands at three-quarter speed.
Now play it at full speed, and let the last chord ring.

tips.text: In stride, look at the low octave and let the hand find the chord by feel.
The quick turn around E is a decoration. Play it softer than the tune.
Lift the hand after the B, then land on the last chord with both hands together.

tricky.text: The turn starts on the high G. Fingers 5, 4, 3 and the thumb run down, then finger 2 takes E.
Change to the little finger on the repeated E, and walk down one finger per key. The left hand jumps to the low E.
Finger 2 crosses over the thumb for B. Play it short, and move the hand down for the last chord.
